units.title: Being Responsible
units.intro: Grammar: modal verbs for obligation (must, have to, should) and for inference (must be, can’t be, must have).

cards.title: Modals for obligation and advice
rule: **must / have to** = strong obligation: *You **must** wear a helmet.* **mustn’t** = it is not allowed. **don’t have to** = it is not necessary.
**should / ought to** = advice or duty: *We **should** look after our parents.* All modals are followed by the **base verb** (no to after must/should/can).

examples.text: Students must arrive on time.
You must to finish it.
You don’t have to pay; it’s free.

cards.title: Modals for inference
rule: When we are almost sure something is true: **must be**: *He has worked all day. He **must be** tired.* Almost sure it is not true: **can’t be**: *That **can’t be** Lula; she is in Keren.*
About the past: **must have + past participle**: *The ground is wet. It **must have rained**.* **can’t have + pp**: *She **can’t have seen** us.*

examples.text: The lights are off. They must be asleep.
She must has left.

cards.pattern: must be / can’t be  ·  must have + past participle

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **Must** = 99% sure or a rule; **can’t** = 99% sure it’s not; add **have + pp** to look back.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Must/have to show obligation, should gives advice, mustn’t forbids, don’t have to means not necessary. For inference use must be / can’t be (present) and must have / can’t have + past participle (past).

glossary.meaning: A helping verb such as must, should, can that adds meaning.
A conclusion based on evidence.

tips.text: **Must** = 99% sure or a rule; **can’t** = 99% sure it’s not; add **have + pp** to look back.

units.title: Adventure
units.intro: Grammar: gerunds (-ing as a noun), infinitives (to + verb), participles, and the future continuous.

cards.title: Gerunds, infinitives and participles
rule: A **gerund** (verb + -ing) works as a noun: ***Camping** is fun.* After prepositions and verbs like *enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, can’t help*, use the gerund: *I enjoy **climbing**.*
An **infinitive** (to + verb) follows verbs like *want, decide, hope, plan, attempt, agree*: *They decided **to camp**.* It also shows purpose: *She went out **to buy** bread.*
**Participles as adjectives:** -ing describes the cause (*an **amazing** trip*); -ed describes the feeling (*We were **amazed***).

examples.text: I avoid travelling at night.
She wants going home.
The story was horrifying; we were horrified.

cards.title: Future continuous
rule: **will be + -ing** = an action in progress at a future time: *This time tomorrow we **will be climbing** the mountain.* It is also used for planned future events: *I **will be meeting** him at noon.*

examples.text: At 8 tomorrow I will be travelling to Keren.
At 8 tomorrow I will travelling.
examples.fix: At 8 tomorrow I will be travelling.

cards.title: Common mistakes
head: Wrong
Right
Why

I was very bored in class.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **After a preposition, always -ing.** The **-ing** thing causes the **-ed** feeling.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Gerunds act as nouns and follow prepositions and verbs like enjoy/avoid/finish; infinitives follow verbs like want/decide/hope and show purpose. -ing adjectives describe causes, -ed adjectives feelings. Future continuous (will be + -ing) describes an action in progress at a future time.

glossary.meaning: A verb + -ing used as a noun.
to + base verb.
will be + verb-ing.

tips.text: **After a preposition, always -ing.** The **-ing** thing causes the **-ed** feeling.

units.title: Writing Creatively
units.intro: Grammar: noun clauses as objects and complements, and a review of modal verbs.

cards.title: Noun clauses
rule: A **noun clause** does the job of a noun. It often begins with **that, what, whether/if, who, where, why, how**.
**Object position:** *I know **that he is honest**.* *She asked **where the library was**.* **Complement position** (after be): *The problem is **that we have no time**.* *That is **what I wanted**.*
In a noun clause from a question, use **statement order**: *I don’t know **where she lives*** (not *where does she live*).
**Sequence of tenses:** after a past main verb, the noun clause usually moves into the past: *He said **that he was** ready.*

examples.text: I believe that she will win.
Tell me what is your name.
examples.fix: Tell me what your name is.

examples.text: The truth is that we were late.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: In a noun clause the question **turns into a statement**: wh-word + subject + verb.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Noun clauses (that/wh-/if) act as objects or complements. Inside them use statement word order, and follow the sequence of tenses after a past main verb. Modals (can, could, may, might, must, should) are followed by the base verb.

glossary.meaning: A clause that acts as a noun (subject, object or complement).
Words after be that complete the meaning of the subject.

tips.text: In a noun clause the question **turns into a statement**: wh-word + subject + verb.

units.title: Brain Drain
units.intro: Grammar: the subject–verb–complement (SVC) pattern and clauses: noun phrases, noun clauses, adjective (relative) clauses and adjectival complements.

cards.title: SVC sentences and adjectival complements
rule: **SVC:** Subject + linking verb (*be, become, seem, look, feel*) + Complement (a noun or adjective that describes the subject): *Many graduates **became** doctors.* *The problem **seems** serious.*
An **adjectival complement** follows an adjective: *I am **happy to help**.* *She is **sure that she will return**.*

examples.text: The situation became serious.
The situation became seriously.

cards.title: Adjective (relative) clauses
rule: An **adjective clause** describes a noun and begins with **who** (people), **which** (things), **that** (people or things), **whose** (possession), **where** (places), **when** (time): *Doctors **who leave the country** are hard to replace.*
**Defining** clauses tell us which one (no commas). **Non-defining** clauses add extra information (with commas; never *that*): *Asmara, **which is the capital**, is clean.*

examples.text: The engineer who designed the dam is Eritrean.
The book what I read was good.
examples.fix: The book that/which I read was good.

examples.text: My uncle, who lives abroad, sends money.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **WHO** for people, **WHICH** for things, **WHERE** for places, **WHOSE** for owners.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: SVC sentences use a linking verb plus a complement (noun or adjective). Adjective clauses (who, which, that, whose, where, when) describe nouns; non-defining ones have commas and never use that. Adjectival complements complete adjectives (eager to, sure that).

glossary.meaning: A verb like be, seem, become that links the subject to a complement.
who, which, that, whose: starts an adjective clause.

tips.text: **WHO** for people, **WHICH** for things, **WHERE** for places, **WHOSE** for owners.

units.title: Expenses
units.intro: Grammar: modals for inference about the future and the present (will be, might be, should be) and adverbial phrases and clauses.

lessons.title: Modals of inference: will, should, might

cards.title: Modals of inference: will, should, might
rule: **will (be)** = very sure: *Prices **will be** higher next year.* **should (be)** = expected / probable: *The loan **should be** approved by Friday.* **might / may (be)** = possible: *We **might** need extra money.*
**won’t** = sure it will not happen; **might not** = possibly not.

examples.text: The bill should arrive tomorrow.
It might to rain.

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Purpose / type
Linker
Example
rows: He might be at the bank.
I walk so that I save money.
Write it down lest you forget.
Although it was cheap, I didn’t buy it.

cards.title: Adverbial phrases and clauses
rule: An **adverbial** tells how, when, where, why or on what condition. A **phrase** has no subject + verb (*in the morning, to save money*). A **clause** has one (*because prices rose, so that we can save, although she earns a lot*).

Purpose: **so that / in order to / to**; negative purpose: **so as not to / lest** (formal, + should or base verb): *Save money **lest** you **(should) fall** into debt.* Contrast: **although / even though**.

examples.text: She saves money in order to buy a house.
Although he earns little but he saves.
examples.fix: Although he earns little, he saves.

examples.text: Work hard lest you fail.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Will = very sure, should = expected, might/may = possible, all + base verb. Adverbial phrases and clauses add time, reason, purpose (so that, in order to), negative purpose (lest, so as not to) and contrast (although).

glossary.meaning: A clause that acts like an adverb (when, because, although, so that...).
For fear that; introduces negative purpose.

units.title: Following Instructions
units.intro: Grammar: identifying parts of speech through affixes, and direct and indirect questions.

cards.title: Parts of speech from affixes
rule: Suffixes often show the part of speech. **Nouns:** -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -er/-or (*instruction, payment, kindness, ability, baker*). **Adjectives:** -ful, -less, -ous, -able, -ive, -al (*useful, careless, famous, reliable, active, national*). **Verbs:** -ise/-ize, -en, -ify (*organise, shorten, clarify*). **Adverbs:** -ly (*carefully*).
Inflectional endings change form, not class: -s (plural/3rd person), -ed (past), -ing, -er/-est (comparison).

examples.text: Please clarify the instructions.
Follow the instructions careful.

head: Suffix
Part of speech

cards.title: Direct and indirect questions
rule: **Direct:** *Where is the station?* **Indirect** (more polite) begins with *Could you tell me..., Do you know..., I wonder...* and uses **statement order** with no do/does/did: *Could you tell me **where the station is**?*
Yes/no questions become **if/whether**: *Do you know **if the shop is open**?*

units.title: Fashion
units.intro: Grammar: the present continuous for actions continuing over a period, and confusing verbs (accept/except, adapt/adopt).

lessons.title: Present continuous for a period of time

cards.title: Present continuous for a period of time
rule: **am/is/are + -ing** describes actions happening now **or around now**, over a period: *Young people **are wearing** traditional clothes again this year.* It also shows changing trends: *Fashion **is becoming** more expensive.*
State verbs (*know, like, want, belong, understand*) are not normally used in the continuous: *I **like** this dress* (not *am liking*).

cards.title: Confusing verbs
rule: **accept** = agree to take (*accept a gift*); **except** = not including (preposition: *everyone **except** me*).
**adapt** = change to suit (*adapt to a new climate*); **adopt** = take as your own (*adopt a new style; adopt a child*).

body: Present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) is for actions in progress now or over a current period and for trends; state verbs stay simple. Accept (verb) vs except (not including); adapt (change to suit) vs adopt (take as your own).

units.title: Making the Right Choices
units.intro: Grammar: a review of tenses, confusing verbs, and the present simple in newspaper headlines.

cards.title: Tense review
rule: **Present simple:** habits and facts (*Water **boils** at 100 °C*). **Present continuous:** now. **Past simple:** finished past. **Present perfect** (have/has + pp): past actions connected to now, with *ever, never, already, yet, just, recently, since, for*: *I **have recently finished** my exams.*
**Future perfect** (will have + pp): completed before a future time: *By June I **will have finished** Grade 10.*

examples.text: She has lived here since 2015.
I have seen him yesterday.
By 2030 we will have built many schools.

cards.title: Headlines in the present simple
rule: Newspaper headlines use the **present simple** for recent past events and leave out small words (*a, the, is*): ***Students Win** National Prize* = Students have won a national prize. A **to-infinitive** shows the future: ***Minister To Open** New School*. A past participle alone shows the passive: ***Bridge Opened** In Keren*.

examples.text: Headline: Team Wins Cup
Headline: Bridge Opened In Keren (= a bridge has been opened)

cards.title: Common mistakes
head: Wrong
Right

rows: I have finished it last week.

By June I will have finished it.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **Yesterday / ago → past simple. Since / for / yet → present perfect. By + future → will have done.**

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Choose tenses by their signal words: habits/facts (present simple), now (continuous), finished past (past simple), past linked to now (present perfect), finished before a future time (future perfect). Headlines use the present simple for recent events and to + verb for the future.

glossary.meaning: has/have + past participle; links the past and now.
The title of a newspaper story.

tips.text: **Yesterday / ago → past simple. Since / for / yet → present perfect. By + future → will have done.**

units.title: Living in Peace
units.intro: Grammar: comparison with as ... as, the same as, different from, and comparative and superlative forms.

cards.title: Making comparisons
rule: **as + adjective + as** = equal: *Peace is **as important as** food.* **not as/so ... as** = less: *War is **not as** cheap **as** people think.*
**the same as** / **similar to** = no difference; **different from** = not the same: *My view is **different from** yours.*
**Comparatives:** short adjectives + -er (*calmer*), long adjectives more + adj (*more peaceful*), + **than**. **Superlatives:** the + -est / the most.

examples.text: Asmara is as cool as Mendefera.
This is different than that.
Peace is more valuable than gold.
She is more taller than me.

cards.pattern: as + adj + as  ·  the same as  ·  different from  ·  -er/more ... than

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Use as ... as for equality, not as ... as for less, the same as for identity, different from for difference, -er/more ... than for comparatives and the -est/the most for superlatives.

glossary.meaning: Form used to compare two things: -er or more.

tips.text: **AS goes with AS; -ER/MORE goes with THAN; SAME goes with AS; DIFFERENT goes with FROM.**
